title: Pointwise Koszul regularity of an immersion after extension of the ground field
statement: Let $K/k$ be a field extension [def-pc-field-extension]. Let $P$ be a scheme [def-pc-scheme] locally of finite type over $k$ [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and let $i:Z\to P$ be an immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion] of $k$-schemes. Put $P_K=P\times_{\operatorname{Spec}k}\operatorname{Spec}K$ and $Z_K=Z\times_{\operatorname{Spec}k}\operatorname{Spec}K$, with induced immersion $i_K:Z_K\to P_K$ and projection $a:Z_K\to Z$ [def-pc-fibre-product]. An immersion is Koszul-regular near a source point if, on some open neighbourhood of it, it is locally a closed immersion into an open subscheme of its target whose ideal is generated by a finite Koszul-regular sequence [def-weil-pbc-koszul-regular-sequence]; empty sequences are allowed. For every $z_K\in Z_K$, the immersion $i_K$ is Koszul-regular near $z_K$ if and only if $i$ is Koszul-regular near $a(z_K)$. Neither finiteness nor separability of $K/k$ is required.

source.place: Tag 0694 (lemma-descending-property-regular-immersion), Koszul-regular clause, pointwise field-extension consequence used in more-morphisms.tex lemma-base-change-lci-fibres. Pointwise passage uses that the projection after a field extension is flat and universally open: morphisms.tex lemma-scheme-over-field-universally-open.

proof.text: Fix $z_K$, write $z=a(z_K)$, and put $p=i(z)$ and $p_K=i_K(z_K)$. Factor the immersion through an open subscheme $U_0\subseteq P$ as a closed immersion and choose an affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq U_0$ containing $p$. Then $Z_U=Z\times_P U=\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)$ for an ideal $I\subseteq A$. Working near $z$ loses no information: every source open neighbourhood in the closed subspace $Z_U$ is $Z_U\cap O$ for some ambient open $O\subseteq U$. Intersecting $O$ with the target open in a local Koszul-regular presentation therefore makes that presentation the restriction of $Z_U\to U$. The same observation applies upstairs. For any affine $W=\operatorname{Spec}B\to U$, the pulled-back closed immersion is $\operatorname{Spec}(B/IB)\to\operatorname{Spec}B$, by the quotient base-change statement. These identifications are of schemes and ideals, not only of point sets.

Let $q:P_K\to P$ be the projection. The morphism $\operatorname{Spec}K\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is flat, so $q$ is flat by stability of flatness under base change. Suppose $i$ is Koszul-regular near $z$. Restrict to a source neighbourhood and target open witnessing this, and base change them along the field extension. The flat-ascent clause for Koszul-regular immersions makes the resulting immersion Koszul-regular. Its source is an open neighbourhood of $z_K$: the inverse image of the chosen source neighbourhood contains $z_K$, since it maps to $z$. Thus $i_K$ is Koszul-regular near $z_K$.

source.place: Tag 067P (lemma-flat-base-change-regular-immersion); flat projection from morphisms.tex Tag 01U9 (lemma-base-change-flat)

proof.text: Conversely suppose $i_K$ is Koszul-regular near $z_K$. Apply the affine neighbourhood criterion to its closed-immersion presentation in $U_K=q^{-1}(U)$, after the ambient shrinking explained in step 1. It gives an affine open $W=\operatorname{Spec}B\subseteq U_K$ containing $p_K$ such that the ideal of the restricted closed immersion is generated by a finite Koszul-regular sequence $f_1,\ldots,f_r\in B$. With $\varphi:A\to B$ induced by $q$, the quotient base-change statement identifies this ideal with $IB$. In particular the regular sequence generates the extended ideal of the original closed immersion, not an unrelated ideal on $W$.

The projection $q$ is open: apply the universally-open-over-a-field statement to the $k$-scheme $\operatorname{Spec}K$ and the $k$-scheme $P$ (interchanging the two fibre-product factors). Consequently $V=q(W)$ is an open neighbourhood of $p$ in $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$. The principal-open basis gives $h\in A\setminus\mathfrak p$ with $p\in D(h)\subseteq V$, where $\mathfrak p$ is the prime of $p$. Let $b=\varphi(h)$, $A'=A_h$ and $B'=B_b$. Principal-open localization identifies $D(h)=\operatorname{Spec}A'$ and $W\cap q^{-1}(D(h))=D_W(b)=\operatorname{Spec}B'$. The inverse-image equality follows directly from $h\notin\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)$ if and only if $\varphi(h)\notin\mathfrak q$.

The morphism $\operatorname{Spec}B'\to\operatorname{Spec}A'$ is surjective: for any $x\in D(h)\subseteq q(W)$ choose $w\in W$ above $x$; its image lies in $D(h)$, so $w\in D_W(b)$. Both are affine opens of the source and target of the flat morphism $q$ from step 2. The affine criterion for flatness therefore gives flatness of $A'\to B'$. The flat-and-surjective-spectrum criterion now makes $A'\to B'$ faithfully flat. Notice that it is this restricted map, rather than the possibly nonsurjective $W\to U$, to which descent will be applied.

source.place: Tag 01U5 (lemma-flat-characterize); algebra.tex Tag 00HQ (lemma-ff-rings), equivalence of flat faithful flatness and surjectivity on spectra

proof.text: Put $J=IA'$. Localization $B\to B'$ is flat, so the images of $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ remain Koszul-regular by flat ascent of Koszul-regular sequences. They generate $IB'=JB'$: both extended ideals consist of finite sums of images of elements of $I$ times elements of $B'$. Thus the hypothesis of faithfully flat descent of locally Koszul-regular ideals holds for $A'\to B'$ and $J$, at every prime above $J$; in its statement one may take the localizing element $1\in B'$ because a regular generating sequence already exists globally on $B'$. At the prime $\mathfrak p A'\supseteq J$ it yields $t\in A'\setminus\mathfrak p A'$ and a finite Koszul-regular sequence generating $J(A')_t$.

The affine open $D_{\operatorname{Spec}A'}(t)$ contains $p$ and is also an open subscheme of $P$, since $\operatorname{Spec}A'=D_U(h)\subseteq U\subseteq P$. On it the original closed immersion has ideal $J(A')_t$, by the quotient base-change statement. The affine Koszul-regularity criterion and the sequence obtained in step 6 therefore show that $i$ is Koszul-regular near $z$. Together with step 2 this proves both implications at the specified point. All steps allow $r=0$; if $Z_K$ is empty there is no point to check. The argument uses only that $K/k$ is a field extension, so it introduces neither a finite-degree nor a separability hypothesis.
